# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and classification

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) results from the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium, producing a progressive, infiltrative, and ultimately restrictive cardiomyopathy. CA has two main subtypes, transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR) and immunoglobulin light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL), with ATTR further differentiated into wild-type (wtATTR) and hereditary (hATTR), depending on the absence or presence of mutation in the transthyretin gene. In ATTR, amyloid fibril formation results from a destabilizing mutation in hereditary ATTR amyloidosis or from an aging-linked process in wild-type ATTR amyloidosis. The most common pathogenic hereditary variant in this context is described where ATTR-cardiomyopathy can occur in the context of genetically normal protein (wild type) or due to genetic mutations, most commonly isoleucine substitution for valine at position 122. AL amyloidosis, in contrast, is a plasma-cell dyscrasia in which systemic immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis is characterized by deposition of amyloid fibrils of light chains produced by clonal CD38+ plasma cells.

## Epidemiology

Long regarded as rare, CA—particularly wtATTR—is now recognized as an under-diagnosed cause of heart failure in older adults [4]. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is an under-recognized cause of heart failure in older adults, resulting from myocardial deposition of misfolded transthyretin (TTR) or pre-albumin. A landmark autopsy and imaging series demonstrated that up to 10% to 15% of older adults with heart failure may have unrecognized wtATTR. Pioneering work established that wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis is a cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The shifting epidemiology reflects the fact that the increased recognition of disease with the improvement in diagnostic armamentarium and serendipitous advancements in the therapeutic landscape have changed the status of CA from being a rare and untreatable disease to being a not-so-rare and treatable disease.

## Clinical presentation and diagnosis

Because amyloid is a multisystem disease, since amyloid fibrils can deposit in multiple organs, multidisciplinary care is a requisite. Clinical red flags include increased left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of hypertension or valvular heart disease, heart failure symptoms, diastolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, and conduction system disease; associated features, including carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis, raise suspicion and may afford a means for early diagnosis. Imaging is central: characteristic patterns of echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance can strongly suggest the disease but are not diagnostic; the diagnosis can be made with noninvasive nuclear imaging when there is no evidence of a monoclonal protein. The diagnostic value of nuclear imaging was first systematically described in 2005 [9], and a pivotal multicenter study transformed practice: bone scintigraphy enables the diagnosis of cardiac ATTR amyloidosis to be made reliably without the need for histology in patients who do not have a monoclonal gammopathy. Crucially, the combined findings of grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy and the absence of a monoclonal protein in serum or urine had a specificity and positive predictive value for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis of 100%. An evolving multidisciplinary consensus continues to refine diagnostic algorithms [11,12].

## Staging and prognosis

Cardiac biomarkers underpin prognostication in AL amyloidosis. A widely used model showed that incorporation of serum free light chain difference into the current staging system improves risk stratification for patients with AL amyloidosis and will help develop risk-adapted therapies. The European position statement and AHA scientific statement provide complementary frameworks for evaluation and management [11,12].

## Treatment

For ATTR-CM, transthyretin stabilizers represent a major advance. In the landmark trial, the primary outcome of all-cause death occurred in 29.5% of the tafamidis group compared with 42.9% of the placebo group. Tafamidis acts because it binds to transthyretin, which prevents tetramer dissociation and amyloidosis. More recently, the next-generation stabilizer acoramidis was studied: acoramidis is a high-affinity TTR stabilizer that acts to inhibit dissociation of tetrameric TTR and leads to more than 90% stabilization across the dosing interval. RNA-targeting therapies that suppress hepatic TTR production have also entered cardiology. In the patisiran cardiac trial, treatment with patisiran in patients with variant or wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis over 12 months preserved functional capacity, health status, and quality of life. Subsequently, in a larger outcomes trial, the use of vutrisiran resulted in lower risk of cardiovascular events and death from any cause compared with placebo. Open-label extension data suggest durability, with early initiation and continuous use of acoramidis associated with sustained clinical benefits in a contemporary transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy cohort. Broader treatment landscapes are summarized in recent reviews [16].

For AL amyloidosis, treatment targets the underlying plasma-cell clone. The main modalities of treatment in AL amyloidosis are chemotherapy and/or autologous stem cell transplantation targeting the underlying plasma-cell clone responsible for AL amyloid formation. The addition of anti-CD38 therapy markedly improved responses: the primary endpoint of hematologic complete response was achieved in 53.3% of the D-VCd arm versus 18.1% of the VCd arm. Carefully selected patients may benefit from advanced surgical options, since heart transplantation in carefully selected patients can be an effective therapeutic option.

## Conclusion

CA has evolved from a rare, untreatable diagnosis to a recognized and treatable cause of heart failure. Heightened clinical suspicion, judicious use of noninvasive imaging, and timely initiation of disease-modifying therapy are paramount, as therapy for ATTR-CM may be most effective when administered before significant cardiac dysfunction. Nonetheless, there is a critical need for continued research and enhanced policy support to refine diagnostic strategies and develop effective treatments.
